content.9.2.2_Technical_considerations_specific_: Patient profile (need for emergency or very urgent revascularization) influences CABG technique (including on-pump beating heart CABG) and choice/use of CABG conduits. Prompt surgical revascularization in emergencies limits use of full arterial revascularization because of time for graft harvesting. Total venous graft-based CABG or single left internal mammary artery plus additional venous grafts may be useful in this setting.
content.9.3_Spontaneous_coronary_artery_dissecti: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is an infrequent cause of ACS overall but accounts for a significant proportion of ACS cases in young/middle-aged women. Pathophysiology differs from Type 1 MI and management/outcomes differ. Accurate diagnosis is paramount. Until prospective trial evidence is available, patients with SCAD should receive the same pharmacological therapy as other ACS patients.
content.9.3.1_Intravascular_imaging: No randomized controlled trials guide management of SCAD; use of intravascular imaging (OCT or IVUS) is based on cohort studies and expert opinion. In diagnostic uncertainty after angiography, intracoronary imaging may be considered but only if sufficient diagnostic uncertainty exists and other factors (vessel tortuosity, diameter, distal lesion location) do not make instrumentation prohibitively risky. If intravascular imaging is performed, ensure the guide wire is within the true lumen before advancing the imaging catheter. In patients with SCAD managed medically, additional coronary instrumentation and intravascular imaging is not recommended on safety grounds.
content.9.3.2_Revascularization: Conservative medical management is generally recommended for SCAD rather than PCI. International case series report coronary complications following PCI in >30% of patients. A pooled analysis of three SCAD–PCI cohorts (215 patients, 94% female) and a matched conservatively managed cohort (n = 221) found PCI was associated with complications in approximately 40% of cases (including ~13% with serious complications). PCI is recommended only for SCAD with symptoms/signs of ongoing myocardial ischaemia, a large area of myocardium at risk, and reduced antegrade flow. Useful interventional strategies include minimal plain balloon angioplasty to restore flow followed by a conservative strategy, targeted stenting to seal proximal and distal ends of the dissection, and/or extended stent lengths to prevent propagation of the dissection.
